report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Summary

Preliminary update - the information in this report is based on the evidence available at the time of writing and may change as the investigation proceeds.

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026 (local time, UTC+8) a 220 t class rigid [the other attendee 1], descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 open pit at Bindarra Gold Mine empty, struck the right side of a light vehicle (LV-118) coming out of the RL 312 dewatering spur. The impact was at 24 km/h after braking from 37 km/h. The light vehicle was pushed about 18 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side. The driver suffered a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax, was extricated at 03:14 and flown out at 07:40. The light vehicle was destroyed and the Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes. The occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury. The investigation is under way and this update makes no findings. A site-wide positive-call direction is in force and the spur remains closed.

What we know

The 220 t class rigid [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] was descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 pit empty when, at 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026, it collided with a light vehicle (LV-118) coming out of the RL 312 dewatering spur.

The spur is a 240 m access road to dewatering bore DW-14. It was cut under works order WO-26-4471, completed on 31/07/2026, and first used by light vehicles on 02/08/2026. It joins the main ramp on the [the other attendee 1]'s left, 34 m below a convex grade break that the crews call the crest. The ramp runs on a 9.1 per cent descending grade. The collision happened in darkness, because there is no fixed lighting in the Stage 4 pit. The light vehicle carried one occupant, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor, who was on the third of three night shifts at the mine (09/08, 10/08 and 11/08).

Before the collision, a dewatering technician had submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 at 23:48 on 04/08/2026. It described a near miss at the same spur at about 22:10 that night, and the report was closed on 06/08/2026.

The intersection had no warning sign on either ramp approach, no give-way or stop control at the spur mouth, no delineation and no posted speed. A construction sign at the spur mouth was removed on 02/08/2026 and nothing replaced it. The in-cab road network, last published on 24/07/2026, showed no intersection at RL 312. A survey on 13/08/2026 measured the available sight distance at the intersection at 41 m. The stopping distance of the [the other attendee 1] at the posted speed is 96 m, and the traffic management plan sets a minimum of 120 m.

The pit channel was logged continuously. The [the other attendee 1] driver called, and was acknowledged, at the RL 360 crossover at 02:46:21. Neither driver made a positive radio call before the RL 312 intersection, and the spur is not one of the nine intersections at which the traffic management plan requires a call. Neither driver knew the other was there until the [the other attendee 1] came over the crest and the driver saw the light vehicle's beacon, about 53 m above the spur.

The [the other attendee 1]'s recorded data gave a last steady data point at 02:47:06, at 37 km/h and 53 m above the spur mouth. About 1.4 seconds later the service brakes were applied, the retarder went to maximum and the [the other attendee 1] was steered right, towards the wall. At 02:47:09.2 the collision awareness system logged a proximity event at 21.4 m and raised no alert, and the log records the alert as suppressed by a geofence. The impact was at 24 km/h. The [the other attendee 1]'s front left struck the right side of the light vehicle, pushed it about 18 m down the ramp and rolled it onto its left side against the inner windrow. The [the other attendee 1] stopped 19 m below the intersection.

Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic at 02:48:01, and the emergency response team was paged at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54. The second responder arrived at 03:07, and the driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision. The driver was conscious throughout, reached the surface medical facility at 03:41 and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. The injuries were a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax.

The light vehicle was destroyed. The [the other attendee 1] was damaged at the front left and returned to service on 14/08/2026. The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes, and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. The occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury. The [the other attendee 1] driver and the shift supervisor were both tested for drugs and alcohol, and both results were negative.

Brake tests on the [the other attendee 1] on 03/08/2026 and 14/08/2026 gave 0.80 and 0.82 m/s2, and the occurrence download gave 0.78 m/s2. The ramp surface was dry and no precipitation was recorded. A wet or slippery surface and reduced brake performance were each examined and are very unlikely.

What we are looking at

The following areas are being examined.

  • How the RL 312 spur came to be opened to traffic. Works order WO-26-4471 classified the work as routine earthworks under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3, so no management of change record was raised, and the handover field reads N/A. Of 14 new Stage 4 roads cut since the 12/11/2025 review, 3 were raised under a management of change record and 11 under a works order, and this difference is being examined.
  • How the traffic management plan lists positive-call intersections and when it is reviewed. BIN-TMP-004 lists nine intersections at Appendix B and is reviewed annually, with the next review due 12/11/2026. The way Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 treats review and the nomination of those intersections is also being examined.
  • Intersection controls and sight distance. The survey gave 41 m of sight distance at the spur against a stopping distance of 96 m, and the intersection had no warning sign, give-way control or delineation. These are being examined against clauses 6.2 and 6.4 of BIN-TMP-004.
  • The collision awareness system suppression geofence and what operators were told about it. Across the Stage 4 [the other attendee 1] fleet, 68 proximity events were suppressed inside the S4-LOAD geofence in 12 months, nine of them involving a light vehicle on the main ramp. No other [the other attendee 1] [the other attendee 1] has yet been asked what they knew of the geofence.
  • Light vehicle access to operating pits. This covers how access cards are issued under ORR-STD-009 clauses 7.3 to 7.5, and the light vehicle driver's training, including the light vehicle pit driving assessment. Whether the Bindarra site supplement was issued is not yet known because Hallorn's own records are outstanding. It also covers whether the night shift supervisor had any means of knowing a light vehicle was in the pit, because the supervisor did not know and said no permit, call-in, board or check exists at pit entry.
  • Night shift rostering, fatigue, dust and emergency response. The roster is 14 nights on and 7 off, and the collision was on night 10 of 14, 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift. Whether the [the other attendee 1] driver was fatigued during the approach is still open and could not be settled. Whether airborne dust on the ramp affected the approach is also still open and could not be settled. The water cart pass was 7 minutes overdue and the dust monitor logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre against a site trigger of 250, while nothing at Bindarra measures visibility. The night shift emergency response is also being examined: one paramedic is rostered and the second responder is called from the village 11 km away. The post-incident review measured a delay of approximately 9 minutes in extrication and recorded no effect on the clinical outcome.

Containment and next steps

Containment measures were put in place on the night of the occurrence, and further interim actions followed. They are reported here as actions taken, not as evidence of any cause.

Actions taken

On 12/08/2026 the Stage 4 pit was stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. The RL 312 spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic that night and remains closed. Both vehicles were isolated and left in position, and the scene was photographed and surveyed before recovery. Data from the fleet management system and the collision awareness system were downloaded from the [the other attendee 1] at 09:30 and provided to the investigation unopened.

At 05:10 on 12/08/2026 the Mining Manager issued a site-wide direction. It requires a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, whether listed in the traffic management plan or not, until further notice. The direction was read at the following four pre-starts and posted beside the Appendix B board in the Stage 4 crib room. It stands until BIN-TMP-004 is amended.

On 14/08/2026 the survey department measured the available sight distance at the other ten unlisted roads cut in Stage 4 since the last plan review. Two of the ten are below the minimum in clause 6.2 of the plan, and both have been closed pending a stop control.

On 28/08/2026 Tarrowen technical services added suppressed proximity events to the monthly collision awareness report, broken down by geofence and by vehicle class. They also re-cut the previous twelve months on the same basis for the Stage 4 fleet. This work is in progress, and the first report is due on 30/09/2026.

Next steps

The investigator in charge has issued three recommendations, each open with a response due on 30/09/2026. They are recommendations only. The first concerns ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3 and the works order form at Schedule 4, so that a new intersection with a [the other attendee 1] road is referred to the plan owner, the survey department and technical services. The second concerns BIN-TMP-004, to provide a route for an intersection to reach Appendix B between annual reviews and to require referral of a new road when it is opened. The third concerns treating a change to a suppression geofence boundary as a change to a documented control, with operators told in writing where the collision awareness system is suppressed.

Several enquiries remain outstanding:

  • Hallorn's own records on whether the site-specific supplement was issued to the light vehicle driver.
  • Whether Tarrowen supervisors have ever been trained on BIN-TMP-004, which is to be put to Tarrowen's training coordinator.
  • Whether technical services told anyone at Orrabinda or Tarrowen of the June 2026 extension of the S4-LOAD geofence.
  • What other [the other attendee 1] operators understood about the system on the ramp, since no other [the other attendee 1] has yet been asked.

One further interview is not yet finalised, and nothing is inferred from it here.

The next scheduled review of the traffic management plan was due on 12/11/2026. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether that review took place]

reviewNotes:
- [What we know] - Timeline entry "First sighting, the beacon at 53 m" lists the factor "Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach to the intersection". That factor does not appear in the causal chains or among the factors named as failing Influence, so its category is not stated. - Causal chain "Truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon appearing" links directly to the critical event with no intermediate step. Braking reduced the collision speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h, so the edge may need its direction or label checked. - Light vehicle departure, timed "about 02:45 to about 02:47 (2 m 06 s)": a precise duration is given between two approximate times. The driver's own "about ten to three" is later than the recorded collision and is correctly set aside. - Distance at first sighting: the operator's interview and safety report give about 40 m, the survey and download give 53 m. Both are reported above. - Push distance: the notification says approximately 18 m and the scene survey says 18.4 m. These are consistent, and the measured figure is used. - The light vehicle driver's interview is not finalised. His statements on speed and on not stopping are summarised as provisional. - [What we are looking at] - "Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection": the Influence test is recorded as Inconclusive, yet the factor carries a "Led to" edge to "Neither driver aware of the other until the truck came over the crest" and appears in that event's "Led from" list. The fatigue factor's notes say an unestablished factor deliberately has no arrow. The dust edge is inconsistent with that approach. - "Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach": the test note says a detailed fatigue assessment "was not pursued". The Evidence gathering checklist answers "[Yes]" to "Is a detailed fatigue assessment required?". The two do not agree. - "Access cards issued with no check of the pit driving assessment": the evidence says it is "not yet known" whether the site supplement was issued, because the contractor's records are outstanding. The approved "What we know" section says "There is no evidence that he completed the site supplement". That wording reads more firmly than the evidence supports. - Approved "What we know" section: it contains several facts not found anywhere in the evidence. These are the operator's estimate of about 40 m, the flight to the trauma centre at 07:40, the hazard report not being referred outside the dewatering department, the departure from the bore collar at about 02:45, and the stand-down durations. Each should be checked against the source extracts. - [Containment and next steps] - Tarrowen suppressed-event reporting action (CAS factor): the first report was due 30/09/2026 but the action is still shown as "In progress". The three investigator recommendations are also still "Open" with responses due 30/09/2026. As of 08/10/2026 these statuses look out of date, so they should be confirmed. - Haul truck operator fatigue (unresolved matter): the test note says a detailed fatigue assessment "was not pursued". The checklist item "Is a detailed fatigue assessment required?" is marked Yes. These two entries conflict. - Investigation log, 2026-09-01 entry: it says the extrication object is pending "the fleet-wide responder roster". The extrication factor's own notes say the outstanding question is the roster "across the other three night shifts on site". The scope of the outstanding enquiry should be reconciled. - Survey action of 14/08/2026 (stop control factor): it refers to "the other ten unlisted roads cut in Stage 4 since the last review". That figure assumes all eleven works-order roads were unlisted and none of the three management-of-change roads was. The record does not state the listing status of the three management-of-change roads.

  • [Summary] - Summary, "Safety issues" list: the roster and the night shift extrication items carry "(unlikely)". That is their Influence grade. Their Importance grades are "likely" and "very likely". If the term appears beside a safety issue, it may be read as a judgement of the issue's importance.
